Wallets and seed phrases: custodial or non-custodial, and how to keep both safe

A wallet is where your crypto is controlled from. Who holds the keys decides who really owns the money, so it is worth understanding before you put anything in.

Two kinds of wallet

  • Custodial. An exchange or app holds the keys for you. You log in with a password. It is easy, but if the company freezes your account, fails or is hacked, you depend on it.
  • Non-custodial. You hold the keys yourself, backed up by a seed phrase. Nobody can freeze it, but nobody can recover it for you either.
  • Hardware wallet. A small device that keeps the keys offline. It is the safest option for larger amounts, but it costs money and needs care.

What a seed phrase is

  • A list of 12 or 24 words that can restore your whole wallet on any device.
  • Anyone who has the words controls all your funds. There is no password reset and no support desk that can undo it.
  • Never type it into a website, a chat or a form. Never photograph it, put it in a cloud note or send it to anyone.
  • No real company, admin or “support agent” will ever ask you for it.
  • If you lose it and lose the device, the funds are gone.

Set up a wallet safely

  1. Get the app from the official source. Open the wallet's official website yourself and follow its link to the store. Check the publisher name, because fake apps copy the logo.
  2. Write the seed phrase on paper, offline, before you deposit anything. Check each word twice.
  3. Keep two copies in separate safe places. A cloud note, a screenshot or a messenger chat is not safe.
  4. Send a small test amount first and confirm it arrives before moving the rest.
  5. Keep small amounts in a phone wallet you use often, and larger savings in a safer place such as a hardware wallet.

Which one should you use?

There is no single right answer. A custodial account is simpler when you are starting, but you trust the company. A non-custodial wallet gives you control but also all the responsibility. Many people use both: a small amount on an exchange for buying and selling, and savings in their own wallet.

If you think your seed phrase leaked

  • Act fast: create a new wallet on a clean device and move your funds there.
  • Do not reuse the old seed phrase for anything.
  • Revoke old approvals from the compromised wallet.
  • Report the incident to the platform involved. Keep screenshots and transaction IDs.
  • Beware of strangers who offer to “recover” your funds for a fee. This is a common second scam.

Tools mentioned in this guide

  • Arkham Intelligence

    Wallet and entity tracking across blockchains with visual explorers.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open Arkham and paste a wallet address or search for a name.
    2. Open the visual explorer to see which addresses and entities the wallet deals with.
    3. Read the labels carefully. An address with no label is unknown, not safe.
    4. Follow the largest transfers and see where the money went, for example an exchange or a new wallet.
    5. If alerts are available, set one for an address you want to watch.

    Linking an address to a real person or company can be wrong. Do not accuse anyone based on a label.

    Level: Intermediate
    Open Arkham Intelligence (opens in a new tab)

  • GoPlus Security

    Checks tokens, contracts and links for common scam and honeypot risks.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the GoPlus website and find its token security checker.
    2. Choose the blockchain network the token lives on, such as Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana or TRON.
    3. Paste the contract address. Copy it from the project's official website or from CoinGecko, not from a chat message, then run the check.
    4. Read the warnings first: honeypot (you can buy but not sell), very high buy or sell tax, an owner who can mint new tokens or change the rules, and hidden owners.
    5. If the report shows several risks, do not buy or approve anything. If it looks clean, remember that is only one input.

    A clean scan is not a guarantee. New scams are built to pass checks, and the tool cannot see the team's plans.

    Level: Beginner
    Open GoPlus Security (opens in a new tab)
